The Barrels: 150+ Toads trafficked as cargo aboard the Vigilance — a supply chain of human beings that required managerial approval.
The Sonic Grid: Prisoners used as living batteries to power dragon-suppressing emitters — the Legion's philosophy made into infrastructure.
158 Living Witnesses: The Aegis Command Riot preserved the intended victims of Order 120, turning a massacre-in-progress into a prosecution.
The Lockdown: Aegis sealing itself after the riot is read by Waluigi as consciousness of guilt.
The Bureaucrat's Defense: Ironhand does not deny the acts; he denies they are crimes, arguing responsibility diffuses across a system. Command responsibility exists to defeat exactly this.
The Jurisdiction Gap: The strongest case in the encyclopedia belongs to the tribunal least able to enforce it — because the defendant still commands an army.
The Thwomp Recommendation: Waluigi's single sanctioned sentence of feeling in an otherwise cold account.
waluigi_final_statement: General Ironhand signed a massacre, ran a trafficking operation, and wired the suffering of his own kingdom's people into the machinery of conquest, and his defense is that none of this is his fault because he only did the paperwork. Waluigi rejects this with every fiber of an objectivity that, for once, aligns perfectly with his hatred. Command responsibility is not a technicality; it is the principle that the hand which signs the order owns the graves the order fills. Ironhand owns them. The barrels, the Sonic Grid, Order 120 — these are not the excesses of a soldier but the outputs of an executive who optimized cruelty and felt administratively pleased with the result. The tribunal cannot yet enforce its verdict, because the defendant still commands an army, and Waluigi will not pretend that documents stop tanks. But documents outlive armies, and this one is now permanent: General Ironhand is guilty, the calm with which he did it is not innocence but the very heart of the offense, and when the balance finally tips — as Speaker L is tipping it — the case will already be built and waiting. Until then, Waluigi maintains his official recommendation that the defendant go sit on a Thwomp. This has been, against all emotional odds, an objective account. WAH.

name: The Koopa Crown v. Kamek, the Fallen Regent
title: The Trial of the Regent Sorcerer: How the Greatest Wizard in Koopa History Awoke a World-Eating Worm, Declared Himself Royalty, and Was Sentenced by the Very King He Betrayed — A Complete and Objective Account by Waluigi, Who Thinks He Should Have Stuck to Kidnapping Plumbers
date: Judgment rendered 1040 BF, upon Bowser's return to the Valley
era: The Raventree Crisis — The Primordial Wyrm Incident
docket: Koopa Crown Judgment (rendered directly by King Bowser)
jurisdiction: The Koopa Crown, exercised personally by King Bowser upon his return
prosecutor: The Koopa Crown (the surviving Troop and the Koopa Resistance)
status: Concluded — Convicted, Sentenced to Eternal Imprisonment
outcome: GUILTY of high treason, reckless endangerment of the world, and the deaths of hundreds of Koopa Troop soldiers. Sentence: eternal imprisonment in the very pit Kamek opened beneath the Valley of Bowser, stripped of his titles and his stolen power. Waluigi finds the sentence poetically appropriate and legally uncomplicated, as Kamek's guilt is not seriously in dispute even by Kamek. The only interesting question is not whether he did it, but whether his reasoning for doing it deserves a hearing. Waluigi grants it one, then dismisses it.
charges: High Treason Against the Koopa Crown
Reckless Endangerment of the Entire World (Unsealing the Primordial Wyrm)
Mass Sacrifice of Koopa Troop Soldiers (Hundreds Dead)
Usurpation (Self-Declaration as 'Regent Sorcerer')
Being Corrupted Into a 30-Foot Puppet, Which Is Embarrassing for Everyone
authors_note: This document was reconstructed by Waluigi from the accounts of the Koopa Resistance — the blue-collar workers, Goombas, and one heroic Demolitions Bob-omb who actually defeated Kamek — as well as surviving Troop testimony and Bowser's own pronouncement of sentence. Waluigi discloses that he holds no particular grudge against Kamek beyond the general Koopa Troop grievances, which frees him to enjoy this case, and enjoy it he does. Unlike the Delfino and assassination files, there is no wrongful conviction here to lament. Kamek is guilty, admits the essential facts, and was brought down in the single most satisfying manner available: by the labor force he considered beneath him. WAH.
summary: Believing brute force could no longer win the coming wars, Kamek — the greatest wizard in Koopa history — dug beneath the castle and broke the seals holding the Primordial Wyrm, a world-eating entity. The magic corrupted him into a 30-foot puppet of the thing he freed. He sacrificed hundreds of Troop soldiers to sustain his power and declared himself the 'Regent Sorcerer.' He was defeated not by a hero but by the Koopa Resistance — unionized laborers, Goombas, and a Demolitions Bob-omb who blew up the anchor crystals sustaining his power. Upon returning from the Shadowfell, Bowser stripped Kamek of his titles and sentenced him to eternal imprisonment in the pit he opened. This is the rare trial in which guilt is uncontested; the case is a study in the seduction of catastrophic reasoning and the justice of being undone by those you despised.
description:
Most trials in this encyclopedia turn on whether the defendant did it. This one does not. Kamek did it. He unsealed the Primordial Wyrm, he sacrificed his own soldiers, he crowned himself, and he was there, thirty feet tall and puppeted, for the whole thing. The facts are not the mystery.

The mystery is the REASONING — how the most intelligent wizard in Koopa history talked himself into the single stupidest decision in Koopa history — and the JUSTICE — how a being of immense arcane power came to be defeated by the people he considered furniture.

## The Logic Of A Reasonable Traitor

Kamek's premise was not insane. It was, in fact, correct: the old Koopa doctrine — kidnap the princess, lose to the plumber, repeat — had never won a real war and never would, and the coming conflicts against the Iron Legion and the Regal Empire would demand more than brute force. On this narrow point, Kamek was RIGHT, and Waluigi hates admitting it.

From this correct premise, Kamek drew the most catastrophic possible conclusion: that if conventional power could not win, he should reach for the biggest power available and worry about the consequences afterward. He unsealed a world-eating worm. Waluigi notes that 'the plan was sound until the god-worm' is the most common epitaph in this encyclopedia, and Kamek wrote the definitive version of it.

## Why This Trial Is A Pleasure To Document

After the anguish of defending rivals and the cold fury of documenting Ironhand, the Kamek case is, frankly, a delight. There is no frame, no cover-up, no wrongful conviction. There is only a brilliant man undone by his own arrogance and defeated by a Bob-omb with a demolition charge and a grudge. Waluigi documents it with a light heart and a slight smile.

sections.name: The Premise That Was Right
sections.overview: Kamek's defense, such as it is, rests on the correctness of his starting analysis. Waluigi grants the premise its due — and then demonstrates that a correct premise makes a catastrophic conclusion worse, not better.
sections.waluigi_note: It is tempting to dismiss Kamek as a fool, but he was not a fool, and pretending he was misunderstands the case. He was intelligent, correct about the threat, and therefore fully responsible for the leap he made from correct diagnosis to insane prescription. A fool who blunders into disaster is pitiable. A genius who reasons his way into it is culpable.

subsections.name: The Doctrine Was Genuinely Failing
subsections.description: Kamek looked at the Koopa Troop's strategic position and saw the truth: the old methods were obsolete. Kidnapping and losing had produced a century of stalemate, and the emerging superpowers would not play by the Troop's tired script. Waluigi, who has watched the Troop's schemes fail firsthand and repeatedly, cannot dispute this. The diagnosis was sound. The Troop DID need a new source of strength. Kamek was, up to this exact point, the only strategist in the Valley willing to say so.

subsections.name: The Leap Into The Pit
subsections.description: And then Kamek made the leap that damns him. Confronted with 'our power is insufficient,' he concluded 'therefore I will unseal an ancient world-eating entity and harness it,' which is not strategy but suicide wearing strategy's clothes. Waluigi observes that the distance between Kamek's correct premise and his lethal conclusion is where all his guilt lives. He did not stumble into the Wyrm. He reasoned his way to it, deliberately, with full knowledge that the seals existed for a reason. Correct problems do not justify apocalyptic solutions, and a wizard smart enough to see the problem was smart enough to know better than the solution.

sections.name: The Sacrifice Of The Troop
sections.overview: The gravest of Kamek's crimes is not the reckless unsealing but the deliberate expenditure of hundreds of Koopa Troop lives to sustain his stolen power. Waluigi treats this as the moral center of the case.
sections.waluigi_note: Recklessness endangers; deliberation murders. Kamek did not merely risk his soldiers' lives by awakening the Wyrm. He SPENT them — fed hundreds of loyal Troop members into the machinery of his own ascension. This is the charge that turns a catastrophic blunder into a genuine atrocity.

subsections.name: Loyalty Repaid With Fuel
subsections.description: The Koopa Troop's defining trait is loyalty to its king. Kamek exploited that loyalty and inverted it, redirecting the soldiers' obedience toward his own coronation and then consuming them for power. The hundreds who died did so trusting the chain of command, and Kamek weaponized that trust. Waluigi, who has complicated but real feelings about the Troop, finds this the least forgivable of Kamek's acts. To awaken a worm is stupidity. To feed your own loyal soldiers to it is betrayal of the specific, personal kind that no correct premise can excuse.

subsections.name: The Regent Sorcerer
subsections.description: Having sacrificed the Troop, Kamek crowned himself 'Regent Sorcerer' — a title chosen to imply a legitimacy he did not possess. Waluigi notes the tell: a usurper who must invent a regal-sounding title for himself is confessing that he has no actual claim. 'Regent' implies he governed in trust for another; 'Sorcerer' implies the power was rightfully his. Both were lies. He governed in trust for no one and the power was stolen from a sealed entity that wanted it back. The title is a small crime beside the murders, but Waluigi includes it because self-coronation is always evidence of the exact ambition the defendant will later deny.

sections.name: Defeated By The People He Despised
sections.overview: The most satisfying section Waluigi has written in this entire trial series. Kamek, a being of immense arcane power corrupted into a thirty-foot puppet, was defeated not by a chosen hero but by the Valley's working class. Waluigi savors every word.
sections.waluigi_note: There is a justice in HOW a villain falls, and Kamek's fall is the most just in the encyclopedia. He considered laborers, Goombas, and construction workers beneath his notice — furniture, tools, disposable. And it was precisely these people who ended him, by understanding a thing his genius overlooked: that borrowed power depends on physical anchors, and physical anchors can be demolished on schedule.

subsections.name: The Koopa Resistance
subsections.description: The force that brought Kamek down was the Koopa Resistance — blue-collar workers, Goombas, and the rank-and-file the Regent Sorcerer had discounted entirely. Waluigi cannot overstate how fitting this is. Kamek reached for cosmic power and was defeated by people with tools and a plan. His error was the classic error of the arrogant: he prepared for heroes and gods, and never imagined that the janitors and the demolition crew would simply walk up and unplug him. The Resistance did not out-magic Kamek. They out-worked him.

subsections.name: The Demolitions Bob-omb And The Anchor Crystals
subsections.description: Kamek's stolen power was sustained by anchor crystals — physical objects, and therefore vulnerable to the one profession Kamek had never respected: demolition. A heroic Demolitions Bob-omb blew up the crystals, severing Kamek from the Wyrm's power and collapsing the thirty-foot puppet back into a defeated wizard. Waluigi has documented many defeats. None is more elegant. The greatest wizard in Koopa history was undone by a bomb with a job, applied to a load-bearing crystal, by a member of the labor force he considered disposable. Waluigi files this under 'unionized labor defeats a god,' and considers it one of the finest entries in the archive.

sections.name: The King's Judgment
sections.overview: Kamek was sentenced not by a court but by Bowser himself, the sovereign he betrayed, exercising the Koopa Crown's authority directly. Waluigi examines the sentence and finds it, for once, exactly right.
sections.waluigi_note: There is an irony Waluigi cannot ignore: Bowser, who elsewhere in this encyclopedia was WRONGLY blamed for the assassination of Peach, here acts as a legitimate and correct judge of a genuine traitor. The convenient villain of the Peach case is the rightful sovereign of the Kamek case. History contains multitudes, and so, apparently, does Bowser.

subsections.name: Imprisonment In The Pit He Opened
subsections.description: Bowser stripped Kamek of his titles and sentenced him to eternal imprisonment in the very pit from which he unsealed the Wyrm. Waluigi admires the precision of the poetry. Kamek's punishment is his crime, inverted: he opened the pit to gain power; he now occupies the pit, powerless. He sought to guard the borrowed strength of a sealed entity; he now guards the door he never should have unlocked. A sentence that turns the crime into the cell is the rarest kind of justice — the kind that needs no explanation because the symmetry explains itself.

subsections.name: The Sovereign's Standing To Judge
subsections.description: Some may question whether Bowser, personally wronged by Kamek, could impartially judge him. Waluigi dismisses the objection. Kamek's guilt is uncontested; the facts are admitted; the only question was the sentence, and a sovereign has the standing to sentence a traitor who tried to usurp his crown and murdered his soldiers. This is not the Regency's emergency tribunal convicting Bowser on convenience. This is a king passing lawful judgment on a confessed traitor, and the difference between the two — between a frame and a fair judgment — is precisely the difference this encyclopedia exists to document.

sections.name: Waluigi's Assessment: The Genius Who Should Have Kidnapped A Plumber
sections.overview: Waluigi closes with his assessment of Kamek, delivered with the ease of a man who, for once, has no rival to defend and no atrocity to grimly catalog — only a brilliant fool to appraise.
sections.waluigi_note: Kamek is the most tragic defendant in this series, not because he was wronged — he was not — but because he was capable of so much and chose the one path guaranteed to waste it. Waluigi respects intelligence and is therefore genuinely irritated by its misuse, and no one in the encyclopedia misused more of it.

subsections.name: The Waste Of A Good Mind
subsections.description: Kamek could see what no other Koopa strategist could: that the old ways were failing and the coming wars would demand something new. That clarity was rare and valuable. He could have reformed the Troop's doctrine, trained new tactics, built alliances, done any of a hundred difficult, patient, effective things. Instead he took the shortcut through the pit, and the shortcut ended, as shortcuts through pits do, in the pit. Waluigi finds this maddening precisely because Kamek was not stupid. Stupidity is forgivable. The deliberate waste of a good mind is not.

subsections.name: He Should Have Stuck To Kidnapping Plumbers
subsections.description: Waluigi's official assessment, entered into the permanent record, is that Kamek should have stuck to kidnapping plumbers. The old doctrine was failing, yes — but a failing doctrine is survivable, and a world-eating worm is not. There is a lesson here that Waluigi extends beyond the Valley: when your methods stop working, the answer is better methods, not apocalyptic ones. Kamek forgot this, reached past every reasonable option straight for catastrophe, and is now furniture in his own crater. He was the greatest wizard in Koopa history. He is now a cautionary tale with a title stripped from it. Waluigi rests his case, lightly, and with a smile. WAH.

timeline.event: Kamek, greatest wizard in Koopa history, concludes correctly that the old Koopa doctrine cannot win the coming wars against the Iron Legion and Regal Empire.
Rather than reform the doctrine, Kamek chooses to seek absolute ancient power. He begins excavating beneath the Valley of Bowser toward the sealed Primordial Wyrm.
Kamek unseals the Primordial Wyrm, a world-eating entity. The magic corrupts him, transforming him into a 30-foot puppet of the thing he freed.
Kamek expends hundreds of loyal Koopa Troop soldiers to sustain his stolen power, exploiting the Troop's defining loyalty and consuming it as fuel.
Kamek declares himself the 'Regent Sorcerer,' inventing a title to imply a legitimacy he does not possess.
The Koopa Resistance — blue-collar workers, Goombas, and a Demolitions Bob-omb — organizes against the Regent Sorcerer, the very laborers Kamek considered beneath him.
The Demolitions Bob-omb destroys the anchor crystals sustaining Kamek's power. Severed from the Wyrm, the 30-foot puppet collapses back into a defeated wizard.
King Bowser returns to the Valley, strips Kamek of his titles, and sentences him to eternal imprisonment in the pit he opened.
Kamek, powerless, becomes the guardian of the door he never should have unlocked. Waluigi records the case as the encyclopedia's cleanest verdict.

notableFeatures: Uncontested Guilt: Unlike the Delfino and assassination cases, Kamek's guilt is not in dispute — he did it, admits the facts, and was present throughout.
The Correct Premise, The Catastrophic Conclusion: Kamek was RIGHT that the old Koopa doctrine was failing, which makes his leap to unsealing a world-eating worm worse, not better.
The Sacrifice Of Hundreds: Kamek deliberately consumed hundreds of loyal Troop soldiers as fuel — the atrocity at the moral center of the case.
The Self-Coronation: 'Regent Sorcerer' was a title invented to fake a legitimacy Kamek did not have — a usurper's confession.
Defeated By Labor: Kamek was undone not by a hero but by the working class he despised — the Koopa Resistance and a Demolitions Bob-omb.
The Anchor Crystals: Kamek's borrowed god-power depended on physical objects, which demolition — the one profession he never respected — simply blew up.
The Poetic Sentence: Eternal imprisonment in the very pit he opened — a punishment that is the crime inverted.

Bowser As Legitimate Judge: The villain wrongly blamed for Peach's assassination is here the RIGHTFUL sovereign judging a genuine traitor — the encyclopedia's clearest contrast between a frame and a fair verdict.
waluigi_final_statement: Kamek is guilty, and for once Waluigi gets to say so without agonizing over a frame or grimacing through a defense he did not want to give. The greatest wizard in Koopa history correctly diagnosed that the old ways were failing and then reasoned his way straight into apocalypse, unsealing a world-eating worm, sacrificing hundreds of loyal soldiers as fuel, and crowning himself with a title he invented to hide the theft. He was defeated — gloriously, appropriately — not by a chosen hero but by the laborers and Goombas and one demolitions Bob-omb he considered beneath him, who understood the one thing his genius missed: that borrowed power rests on anchors, and anchors can be blown up on schedule. Bowser, who elsewhere in this encyclopedia was wrongly blamed for a murder he did not commit, here renders the cleanest and most legitimate judgment in the entire record, sentencing the traitor to eternal imprisonment in the pit he opened. The sentence is the crime, inverted; the justice needs no explanation. Waluigi's only editorial addition is his standing assessment, entered permanently: Kamek should have stuck to kidnapping plumbers. WAH.

name: The Liberated Toads' Inquiry into Dan and the Fireball
title: The Trial of the Corrupted Staff: How a Good Man Killed Thirteen of His Own People, Lost an Arm, and Faced a Community That Had to Decide Whether a Weapon's Crime Is the Wielder's — A Complete and Objective Account by Waluigi, Who Found This One Hard to Be Funny About
date: Convened 1040 BF, after the staff was wrested away
era: The Raventree Crisis — The Liberated Toad Staff Crisis
region: Aboard and around the Liberated Toad community
docket: Liberated Toad Community Inquiry (not a Crown court; a survivor tribunal)
jurisdiction: The Liberated Toads, convened as a community to judge one of their own
prosecutor: The grief of thirteen families, represented by the community
presiding: The Liberated Toad leadership council (Rodger and others)
outcome: The community found that Dan's actions, while the direct cause of thirteen deaths, were the product of magical corruption by his staff rather than intent, and declined to condemn him as a murderer — while refusing to pretend the thirteen did not die. No formal punishment beyond the catastrophic ones the crisis had already inflicted: Dan lost his arm when Green T wrestled the staff away, was shrunk by dark healing magic, and must live among the survivors of the people he killed. Waluigi, who documents this case with unusual restraint, considers the community's judgment wiser than any Crown court would have managed.
charges: The Deaths of Thirteen Liberated Toads (Direct Cause: A Fireball Cast by Dan)
Endangerment of the Community's Souls (the staff nearly consumed them)
The Question Beneath All Others: Was It Dan, or Was It the Staff?
authors_note: This document was assembled by Waluigi from Liberated Toad testimony, the account of the staff crisis, and the record of Green T's intervention. Waluigi wishes to note that this is the trial file he found hardest to write in his usual voice. Waluigi's voice is built for grievance, absurdity, and the puncturing of the powerful, and this case contains none of those things — only a good man, a corrupted weapon, thirteen dead, and a community forced to weigh grief against understanding. Waluigi has therefore restrained the jokes. Not out of solemnity for its own sake, but because thirteen Liberated Toads died, and Waluigi respects the Liberated Toads more than almost anyone in this encyclopedia. WAH, quietly.
summary: Dan was one of the original leaders of the Liberated Toads — a competent organizer who helped build the faction from traumatized barrel survivors into a functioning movement. Then his mage staff corrupted him. He cast a fireball that killed thirteen of his own people and nearly consumed their souls. Green T had to physically wrestle the staff away, and in doing so Dan lost his arm; dark healing magic then shrank him. The Liberated Toads, a community forged in trauma, had to decide what to do with one of their founders who had become the instrument of their worst loss. Their inquiry turned on a single agonizing question: when a corrupted weapon moves a good man's hand, whose crime is it? They judged it tragedy, not murder. Waluigi documents their reasoning with rare restraint and concludes they were right.
description:
Waluigi has documented frames, cover-ups, war crimes, and a wizard who woke a worm. This case is none of those. It is smaller and, in a way Waluigi did not expect, heavier: a good man, a corrupted staff, thirteen dead friends, and a grieving community that had to look at one of its founders and decide what he now was.

Waluigi will not perform his usual routine here. The Liberated Toads earned better than that.

## The Weight Of Thirteen

Thirteen Liberated Toads died in the fireball. These were not abstract casualties in a distant war. They were members of a community that had survived being trafficked in barrels, that had clawed its way from cargo to people, and that had lost thirteen of its own not to the Iron Legion or a dragon but to one of its own founders. The betrayal was not chosen, but the dead were just as dead, and the community could not simply forgive its way past their graves.

## The Question Beneath The Case

Everything in this inquiry reduces to one question, and it is a genuinely hard one: when a weapon corrupts the wielder, whose crime is the result? If the staff moved Dan's hand, is Dan a murderer or a victim? If we say victim, do we insult the thirteen dead? If we say murderer, do we punish a man for an intent he never formed? Waluigi has opinions about most things and delivers them loudly. On this question, Waluigi found himself, for once, uncertain — and impressed that a community of trauma survivors reasoned through it more carefully than most courts of trained magistrates ever would.

sections.name: Who Dan Was Before The Staff
sections.overview: A fair inquiry into what Dan did requires an honest account of who Dan was, because the corruption of a good man is a different event than the exposure of a bad one. Waluigi establishes the character the staff overwrote.
sections.waluigi_note: It matters enormously whether Dan was a villain revealed or a good man corrupted, and the evidence is unambiguous: Dan was good. He built the thing that later grieved him. This is not mitigation invented by the defense; it is the documented history of the community he served.

subsections.name: The Builder Of The Movement
subsections.description: Before the fireball, Dan was one of the original leaders who transformed the Liberated Toads from traumatized barrel survivors into a functional movement. This is not a small thing. Taking people who have been treated as cargo and helping them become a community with structure, purpose, and dignity is genuine, patient, difficult good, and Dan did it. Waluigi notes that the community's willingness to judge him gently was not naive sentiment; it was informed by years of watching Dan choose the community's welfare over his own. The staff did not corrupt a stranger. It corrupted a founder.

subsections.name: Why This Makes It Worse, And Also Different
subsections.description: Dan's goodness cuts both ways, and Waluigi refuses to pretend otherwise. On one hand, it means the fireball was an aberration, not an expression of his character — an argument for mercy. On the other, it means the thirteen dead trusted him, followed him, and were killed by the very person their survival had depended on, which is a specific and terrible kind of loss. The community had to hold both truths: that Dan was good, and that being good did not make the thirteen less dead. Waluigi has found that holding two true and opposed things at once is the hardest work a grieving group can do, and the Liberated Toads did it.

sections.name: The Corruption Of The Staff
sections.overview: The central factual question is whether the staff genuinely corrupted Dan or merely disinhibited him. Waluigi examines the evidence and finds the corruption real, external, and consuming.
sections.waluigi_note: There is a lazy cynicism that says a weapon only reveals what was already in the wielder. Waluigi rejects it in this case, because the evidence shows something acting UPON Dan, not merely through him — a hostile magic with its own hunger, one that nearly consumed the very souls it should, on the cynic's theory, have merely 'released.'

subsections.name: A Magic That Wanted The Souls
subsections.description: The staff did not simply amplify Dan's power; it nearly consumed the souls of the people the fireball struck. Waluigi draws the reader's attention to this, because it is the decisive fact. A weapon that merely disinhibits its wielder does not develop an appetite of its own. The staff's attempt to consume souls is evidence of an external, malevolent agency — a hunger that was the STAFF'S, not Dan's. Dan wanted his community to live; he had spent years ensuring it. The thing that wanted them dead and consumed was the corruption, and the corruption was in the staff.

subsections.name: The Wrestling Away, And The Arm
subsections.description: The clearest proof that the staff was the agent is what it took to stop it: Green T had to physically wrestle the staff away from Dan, and Dan lost his arm in the process. Waluigi notes that a man who is merely misbehaving can be told to stop. A man in the grip of a hostile magic must be physically separated from its source, at grievous cost. The severing of Dan's arm was, in effect, the amputation of the corruption — the community cutting the weapon out of the wielder the only way it could. That it cost Dan a limb is proof of how deeply the staff had its hooks in him.

subsections.name: The Shrinking
subsections.description: The dark healing magic that shrank Dan is the final entry in the ledger of what the staff did to him. Waluigi includes it not as punishment but as evidence of scale: this was not a man who cast a spell and walked away. This was a man physically maimed, magically diminished, and left to live in the reduced form the crisis made of him. Whatever the community decided, the staff had already sentenced Dan to a life inside the wreckage of what it did through him.

sections.name: The Community's Reasoning
sections.overview: The Liberated Toads chose not to try Dan as a murderer, but they did not exonerate him either. Waluigi examines the careful, painful middle path they walked, and defends it as wisdom.
sections.waluigi_note: A Crown court would have wanted a clean verdict — guilty or not, punished or freed. The Liberated Toads, who had learned in the barrels that the world rarely offers clean anything, reached for something more honest and more difficult: a judgment that held Dan responsible as the cause without condemning him as a murderer, and that honored the thirteen without pretending vengeance would return them.

subsections.name: Naming It Tragedy Without Erasing The Dead
subsections.description: The community's judgment was that the fireball was a tragedy produced by corruption, not a murder produced by intent — and crucially, they reached this without pretending the thirteen had not died. Waluigi considers this the heart of their wisdom. It would have been easier to pick a comforting extreme: to call Dan a monster and cast him out, or to call him blameless and move on. Instead they held the unbearable middle: Dan caused the deaths, Dan did not intend them, and both facts remain true forever. The thirteen are mourned as victims of a crime; Dan is treated as the instrument of a crime he did not author. No one is asked to lie.

subsections.name: Punishment Already Inflicted
subsections.description: The community imposed no formal punishment, and Waluigi argues this was not leniency but recognition. What punishment could a survivor tribunal add to what had already happened? Dan lost his arm. Dan was shrunk. Dan must live, every day, among the survivors of the people he killed, carrying the knowledge of it in a diminished body. Waluigi notes that there is no cell crueler than that, and no sentence a court could write that would exceed it. The community understood that Dan's punishment was not something to be decided but something already, permanently, in effect.

subsections.name: The Danger Of The Precedent
subsections.description: Waluigi will not pretend the judgment was without risk, because the Liberated Toads did not pretend so either. To rule that a corrupted weapon absolves the wielder is to open a door: what stops the next wielder from reaching for a cursed staff and claiming the staff did it? The community's answer, as Waluigi reads it, was narrow and careful — this was not a defense to be invoked but a fact to be established, and Dan's years of documented goodness, the staff's demonstrated soul-hunger, and the physical cost of separating him from it were the specific evidence that made corruption credible in his case and would not automatically excuse another. Tragedy is a finding of fact, not a loophole. Waluigi respects that they saw the danger and drew the line.

sections.name: Waluigi's Restrained Assessment
sections.overview: Waluigi closes not with a joke but with an honest appraisal of a case that resisted his usual instruments.
sections.waluigi_note: Waluigi built his voice for grievance and absurdity. This case offered neither, and Waluigi has learned that a historian must occasionally set down his favorite tools and simply tell the truth plainly. This is one of those occasions.

subsections.name: Why Waluigi Did Not Make This Funny
subsections.description: The reader accustomed to Waluigi's routine may have noticed its absence, and Waluigi wishes to explain rather than have it mistaken for a lapse. Thirteen Liberated Toads died. The Liberated Toads are, in Waluigi's genuine estimation, among the most admirable groups in this entire encyclopedia — survivors of the barrels who refused to be disposed of, who became people through sheer collective will. To perform comedy over their thirteen graves would be a cruelty Waluigi is not willing to commit, even in service of his brand. Some losses are owed silence, or as close to silence as a compulsive documentarian can manage.

subsections.name: The Verdict Waluigi Endorses
subsections.description: Waluigi endorses the community's judgment without reservation, which is rare for him. They found the hardest true thing — that Dan caused thirteen deaths and did not murder anyone — and they lived inside that contradiction rather than fleeing to a comfortable lie. A Crown court would have demanded a cleaner answer and produced a worse one. The Liberated Toads, taught by suffering to distrust clean answers, produced justice instead: they mourned the dead as victims, treated Dan as the instrument of a crime authored by his staff, and recognized that the cruelest sentence was the one already served. Waluigi has documented many verdicts. This is one of the few he would not change a word of. WAH.

timeline.event: Dan serves as one of the original leaders of the Liberated Toads, helping transform barrel-trafficking survivors into a functional movement.
Dan comes into possession of a mage staff. Over time, the staff's corruption takes hold, acting upon him with a hostile agency of its own.
Under the staff's corruption, Dan casts a fireball that kills thirteen Liberated Toads and nearly consumes their souls — the community's worst single loss to one of its own.
Green T physically wrestles the staff away from Dan. In the struggle, Dan loses his arm — the corruption cut out of the wielder the only way possible.
Dark healing magic shrinks Dan, leaving him physically diminished as well as maimed.
The Liberated Toad leadership convenes as a community to judge one of its founders, confronting the question of whether a corrupted weapon's crime belongs to the wielder.

The community rules the deaths a tragedy produced by corruption, not a murder produced by intent — mourning the thirteen without exonerating the cause, and imposing no punishment beyond the catastrophic ones already inflicted.

Dan lives among the survivors of the people he killed, carrying the loss in a diminished body. Waluigi records this as the truest sentence in the case: not one the court chose, but one already in effect.

notableFeatures: Thirteen Dead By A Founder's Hand: The community's worst loss to one of its own — not to the Legion or a dragon, but to a corrupted founder.
The Soul-Hunger: The staff nearly consumed the victims' souls, evidence of an external malevolent agency rather than mere disinhibition.
The Arm: Green T had to physically wrestle the staff away, costing Dan his arm — the corruption cut out of the wielder at grievous cost.
The Central Question: When a corrupted weapon moves a good man's hand, whose crime is it? The inquiry turned entirely on this.
Tragedy, Not Murder: The community found Dan the cause but not the author of the deaths — holding both truths without fleeing to a comfortable extreme.
Punishment Already Served: No formal sentence was imposed, because losing an arm, being shrunk, and living among the bereaved exceeded anything a court could add.
The Precedent Line: The community treated 'corruption' as a fact to be proven, not a loophole to be invoked — narrow, careful, and aware of the danger.
Waluigi's Restraint: The only trial file in the series where Waluigi deliberately sets aside comedy, out of respect for the Liberated Toads and their thirteen dead.
waluigi_final_statement: Thirteen Liberated Toads died in Dan's fireball, and Waluigi has documented it without the jokes his voice usually reaches for, because the Liberated Toads are owed better than a punchline over their graves. Dan was good — a founder who built the movement that later grieved him — and the staff that moved his hand was genuinely, externally corrupt, a magic with its own hunger that nearly consumed the souls it struck and that cost Dan his arm to remove. The community faced the hardest question in this entire series of trials: when a corrupted weapon crimes through a good man, whose crime is it? They answered it with a wisdom that shames most trained courts, ruling the deaths a tragedy rather than a murder, mourning the thirteen as victims without pretending Dan was blameless, drawing a careful line so that 'the staff did it' could never become a convenient defense, and recognizing that the cruelest possible sentence — a maimed, diminished life lived among the survivors of the people he killed — had already been passed by the crisis itself. Waluigi endorses their judgment entirely, which he almost never does. Some cases are not about grievance or absurdity. Some are just about grief, and what a good community does with it. WAH, quietly.

name: The Onyx Hand Tribunal: In re Archie Miser (Jurisdiction Contested)
title: The Trial Where the Vampires Were the Fair Court: How a Shadow Tribunal of Blood-Drinking Aristocrats Acquitted Archie Miser and Humiliated the Mages' Guild by Being, Somehow, More Just — A Complete and Objective Account by Waluigi, Who Is Deeply Uncomfortable About All of This
date: Convened 1040 BF, during the Shadowfell displacement
era: The Raventree Crisis — The Planar Fracture
region: The Shadow Estate (dark reflection of Raventree Manor), the Shadowfell
docket: Onyx Hand Tribunal, Shadow Estate Bench (rites and precedents of vampiric law)
jurisdiction: The Onyx Hand, asserting supernatural jurisdiction over magical misconduct within its domain — overruling the Mages' Guild
prosecutor: The Mages' Guild (whose jurisdiction was itself on trial)
presiding: The Onyx Hand Bench (vampiric nobility of House Corvinarus and associated lords)
outcome: Archie Miser ACQUITTED of the Mages' Guild's charges of magical misconduct. More significantly, the Onyx Hand tribunal asserted its own supernatural jurisdiction and OVERRULED the Guild entirely, establishing that within the Hand's domain, the Guild's authority does not run. Waluigi is on record as finding it deeply disturbing that the fairest verdict in this encyclopedia was rendered by a court of blood-drinking aristocrats, and he documents it precisely because that discomfort is instructive.

Unauthorized Use of Arcane Power
The Underlying Real Question: Whether the Mages' Guild's Jurisdiction Is Legitimate At All
authors_note: This document was reconstructed by Waluigi from Onyx Hand tribunal records (written in the ornate, self-satisfied style of people who consider murder a table manner), Guild filings, and the account of the Shadow Estate. Waluigi discloses his discomfort openly: he does not like Archie (a rival-adjacent naming-dispute antagonist), he does not like the Mages' Guild (a two-thousand-gold-for-a-broken-rope bureaucracy he despises), and he REALLY does not like the Onyx Hand (blood-drinking aristocrats who conduct politics through hostage etiquette). This is the rare case where Waluigi dislikes every party involved, which he suspects makes him the most objective possible observer, since he has no one to root for. WAH.
summary: During the Shadowfell displacement, the Mages' Guild brought charges of magical misconduct against Archie Miser. The case was heard not by a Guild court but by an Onyx Hand tribunal — a bench of vampiric nobility in the Shadow Estate — which asserted supernatural jurisdiction, acquitted Archie, and overruled the Guild's authority entirely. The verdict is legally momentous: it established that the Guild's jurisdiction is not universal and can be overridden by a rival power with the will to do so. But the truly unsettling fact, the one Waluigi cannot get past, is that the vampires ran a FAIRER proceeding than the Guild would have. A court of aristocratic predators who consider murder good table manners nonetheless applied its own rules consistently, heard the defense, and reached a defensible verdict — which is more than the Guild, with its suppressed evidence and eighty-five-year silences, has ever managed. Waluigi documents the case as a study in the difference between legitimacy and justice.
description:
Waluigi has documented courts that framed the innocent, courts that convicted on convenience, and courts too powerless to enforce their own verdicts. This case presents the opposite and far more disturbing phenomenon: a court that had no business being fair and was fair anyway.

The Onyx Hand is a vampiric power bloc — blood-drinking aristocrats who conduct politics through formal dinners, blood rituals, hostage etiquette, and the casual violence they consider good manners. They are not the good guys. Waluigi wishes to be extremely clear about that. And yet, when the Mages' Guild dragged Archie Miser before them on charges of magical misconduct, the Onyx Hand tribunal heard the case, applied its own rules, acquitted the defendant, and overruled the Guild — and did all of it with more procedural integrity than the Guild has ever shown.

## The Case That Was Really About Jurisdiction

On the surface, this is a trial about whether Archie Miser committed magical misconduct. Underneath, it is a trial about whether the Mages' Guild gets to decide what magical misconduct IS. The Guild has spent centuries asserting itself as the sole authority on all things arcane. The Onyx Hand tribunal was, in effect, the moment a rival power stood up and said: not here. Not in our domain. Your authority stops at our door.

Waluigi, who despises the Guild's monopolistic bureaucracy with a specific and well-documented passion, found himself in the uncomfortable position of cheering for the vampires — not because the vampires were good, but because watching the Guild's universal jurisdiction get overruled was one of the more satisfying legal spectacles of the crisis.

## Why Waluigi Dislikes Everyone Here

This is the only trial in the series where Waluigi has no one to root for and dislikes all parties equally: Archie (naming-dispute antagonist), the Guild (extortionate bureaucrats), and the Onyx Hand (predatory aristocrats). Waluigi suspects this universal distaste makes him the ideal chronicler, since objectivity is easiest when you want no one to win.

sections.name: The Guild's Charge And Its Real Motive
sections.overview: The Mages' Guild charged Archie Miser with magical misconduct. Waluigi examines the charge and finds that its true purpose was not to punish Archie but to assert the Guild's jurisdiction in a domain where it was being challenged.
sections.waluigi_note: The Guild rarely does anything for the reason it states. Its filings are always, on inspection, about power — about extending, defending, or monetizing its monopoly on the arcane. The Archie charge was no exception. Punishing Archie was the pretext; asserting jurisdiction over the Shadowfell was the point.

subsections.name: The Two-Thousand-Gold Institution
subsections.description: Waluigi reminds the reader of the Guild's character, established elsewhere in this encyclopedia: this is an institution that charges two thousand gold to identify a broken rope, that takes custody of magical evidence and then finds it 'complicated,' that has maintained an eighty-five-year 'no comment' on the assassination forensics. The Guild is not a neutral arbiter of magic. It is a monopoly that treats the arcane as its private revenue stream and its charges as instruments of control. Reading the Archie charge as a good-faith prosecution requires ignoring everything the Guild has ever done.

subsections.name: Jurisdiction As The Prize
subsections.description: The Shadowfell, and the Shadow Estate specifically, is Onyx Hand territory — a domain where the Guild's authority had never been tested. By charging Archie there, the Guild was not merely prosecuting a man; it was planting a flag, asserting that Guild law runs everywhere, even in a vampiric aristocracy's own house. Waluigi recognizes the move because the Guild makes it constantly: expand the monopoly by treating your authority as universal until someone forces you to defend it. This time, someone did.

sections.name: The Onyx Hand Asserts Itself
sections.overview: Rather than surrender Archie to Guild justice, the Onyx Hand convened its own tribunal and claimed jurisdiction. Waluigi examines the assertion and its startling implications for the Guild's supposed universality.
sections.waluigi_note: The Onyx Hand's move was audacious and, Waluigi admits, effective. Faced with the Guild's flag-planting, the Hand did not argue about it. It simply held its own court, on its own ground, under its own law, and dared the Guild to do something about it. Power, when it declines to negotiate, is remarkably clarifying.

subsections.name: The Domain Doctrine
subsections.description: The Onyx Hand's jurisdictional claim rested on a principle Waluigi will call the Domain Doctrine: within the Hand's territory, the Hand's law governs, and no external authority — Guild, Crown, or otherwise — supersedes it. This is, in fact, how sovereignty has always worked; the Guild's pretense of universal jurisdiction was the aberration, not the Hand's assertion of local control. Waluigi notes the irony that it took a court of vampires to articulate a principle of sovereignty that the Guild had spent centuries pretending did not apply to it. The vampires were, on this point, simply correct.

subsections.name: Overruling The Guild
subsections.description: The tribunal did not merely acquit Archie; it overruled the Guild's jurisdiction outright, establishing that the Guild's authority is contingent, not universal — that it can be overridden by a rival power with the standing and the will to do so. Waluigi considers this the most legally consequential single act in the encyclopedia's trial record, because it punctured the Guild's central myth. For centuries the Guild had ruled the arcane by convincing everyone its authority was absolute. The Onyx Hand proved, in one proceeding, that it was merely unopposed — and that the difference between absolute and unopposed is exactly one rival willing to hold its own court.

sections.name: The Uncomfortable Fairness Of The Vampires
sections.overview: The heart of the case, and the source of Waluigi's discomfort: the Onyx Hand tribunal ran a fairer proceeding than the Guild would have. Waluigi documents this reluctantly and honestly.
sections.waluigi_note: Waluigi did not want this to be true. Waluigi wanted the vampire court to be a kangaroo court, a mockery, a blood-soaked farce he could condemn. Instead it applied its own rules consistently, heard the defense, and reached a defensible verdict, which forced Waluigi to confront an idea he finds genuinely upsetting: that a predatory aristocracy can still run a more honest court than a corrupt bureaucracy.

subsections.name: Rules Applied Consistently
subsections.description: The Onyx Hand, whatever its monstrousness, has actual law — precedents, rites, procedures that it follows because its aristocratic self-image depends on following them. The tribunal applied those rules to Archie's case consistently, which is more than can be said for the Guild, whose 'rules' bend reliably toward whatever expands Guild power. Waluigi draws a hard distinction here: the Hand is EVIL but LAWFUL; the Guild is respectable but ARBITRARY. And an evil court that follows its own rules will, on any given case, often produce a more predictable and defensible outcome than a respectable one that follows only its interests. This is a deeply unpleasant thing to have learned, and Waluigi has learned it.

subsections.name: The Defense Was Actually Heard
subsections.description: Unlike the Pianta Bench that convicted Mario at arraignment, or the Regency tribunal that condemned Bowser in absentia, the Onyx Hand tribunal actually heard Archie's defense before ruling. Waluigi finds it almost unbearable that the proceeding which best honored the basic form of a fair trial — a defendant present, a defense heard, a verdict reasoned — was the one convened by blood-drinking predators in a haunted estate. It suggests that the trappings of respectability (a Guild, a Crown, an official seal) are no guarantee of fairness, and that fairness is a PRACTICE, not a pedigree. The vampires practiced it. The Guild did not.

subsections.name: Why This Does Not Make The Vampires Good
subsections.description: Waluigi must guard against the seductive false conclusion that a fair verdict makes the Onyx Hand good. It does not. The Hand hunts party members through corridors, conducts hostage etiquette, and considers murder a table manner; Vivian Corvinarus dropped a weeks-long disguise to hunt the living through the Shadow Estate. A single fair tribunal does not launder a bloc of predators. What it proves is narrower and stranger: that justice and virtue are separable, that a wicked institution can render a just verdict while a respectable one renders unjust ones, and that Waluigi should evaluate courts by what they DO, not by how civilized they claim to be. The vampires did one thing right. They remain, in all other respects, exactly as monstrous as advertised.

sections.name: Waluigi's Assessment: A Case With No Heroes
sections.overview: Waluigi closes his most uncomfortable trial file with an assessment of a proceeding in which he could root for no one and learned something anyway.
sections.waluigi_note: The absence of anyone to cheer for is, Waluigi has decided, the purest condition for a historian. With no ally to protect and no favorite to flatter, Waluigi could look at the case plainly, and what he saw unsettled him more than any frame or atrocity in the series.

subsections.name: The Defendant Waluigi Did Not Want Acquitted
subsections.description: Archie Miser is, in Waluigi's ongoing accounting, an antagonist — the man who calls the party 'the Freeroamer Heroes,' who committed brand theft against the name Disaster Inc., who bleeds entropy and cuts off fingers and calls himself 'Darman Knightly' in the Shadowfell like it is a name a serious person would choose. Waluigi did not want Archie acquitted. But the Guild's charge was a jurisdictional power grab dressed as justice, and the tribunal's acquittal was defensible on the evidence, and Waluigi's dislike of the defendant does not entitle him to prefer a corrupt conviction to a fair acquittal. This is the discipline objectivity demands: sometimes the person you dislike is acquitted by a court you despise, overruling an institution you hate, and the correct response is to report that it was, infuriatingly, handled correctly.

subsections.name: The Lesson Waluigi Did Not Want
subsections.description: The lesson of this case is one Waluigi resisted and ultimately accepted: legitimacy and justice are not the same thing. The Mages' Guild had legitimacy — official standing, universal pretension, the respect of the established order — and used it to pursue a jurisdictional grab. The Onyx Hand had no legitimacy at all — a bloc of predators asserting raw local power — and nonetheless produced the fairer verdict. Waluigi has spent this encyclopedia exposing courts that hid injustice behind respectability, and here is the mirror image: a court that hid a moment of justice behind fangs. Evaluate the verdict, not the pedigree. It is the same lesson every trial in this series teaches, arriving this time from the most disturbing possible direction. Waluigi rests his case, and would like a moment alone. WAH.

timeline.event: The Mages' Guild establishes itself as the self-declared universal authority on all things arcane, treating its jurisdiction as absolute.
Raventree Manor shatters across dimensions. Archie Miser is displaced into the Shadowfell, into the domain of the Onyx Hand and the Shadow Estate.
The Mages' Guild brings charges of magical misconduct against Archie — a prosecution that doubles as an assertion of Guild jurisdiction over Shadowfell territory.
Rather than cede the case, the Onyx Hand convenes its own tribunal in the Shadow Estate, asserting supernatural jurisdiction under its own law.
The tribunal hears Archie's defense and applies its own consistent precedents — a fuller proceeding than the Guild's own courts typically afford.
Archie Miser is acquitted. The Onyx Hand overrules the Guild's jurisdiction entirely, establishing that Guild authority is contingent, not universal.
The precedent stands: a rival power with will and standing can override the Guild. Waluigi files the case as proof that legitimacy and justice are separable.
The Onyx Hand's own house descends into succession war — Vivian Corvinarus hunting party members through the corridors — reminding everyone that a fair court does not make a safe host.

notableFeatures: The Vampires Were The Fair Court: The Onyx Hand tribunal ran a more procedurally sound proceeding than the Mages' Guild would have — the encyclopedia's most unsettling verdict.
Guild Jurisdiction Overruled: The tribunal established that the Guild's authority is contingent, not universal — puncturing the Guild's central myth.
The Domain Doctrine: Within the Onyx Hand's territory, the Hand's law governs — a principle of sovereignty the Guild had pretended did not apply to it.
The Defense Was Heard: Unlike the Mario and Bowser cases, the defendant was present and his defense actually considered before the verdict.
Evil But Lawful vs. Respectable But Arbitrary: The Hand followed its own rules consistently; the Guild bends its rules toward power. Waluigi's central distinction.
Legitimacy ≠ Justice: The case's core lesson — a wicked institution rendered a just verdict while a respectable one pursued an unjust grab.
A Case With No Heroes: The only trial where Waluigi dislikes every party equally, which he argues makes him the ideal chronicler.

Archie Acquitted Against Waluigi's Wishes: A naming-dispute antagonist walked free via a court Waluigi despises overruling an institution he hates — and Waluigi reports it was handled correctly anyway.
waluigi_final_statement: A court of blood-drinking aristocrats acquitted Archie Miser and overruled the Mages' Guild, and the most disturbing sentence Waluigi has written in this entire series is this one: they were fairer than the Guild would have been. The Onyx Hand is monstrous — it hunts the living through its corridors and calls murder a table manner — but it applied its own law consistently, heard the defense, and reached a defensible verdict, which is more procedural integrity than the Guild, with its suppressed evidence and eternal silences, has ever mustered. Waluigi wanted no one in this case to win: not Archie, whom he dislikes; not the Guild, whom he despises; not the Hand, whom he fears. And precisely because he had no one to root for, he could see the lesson clearly, the same lesson every trial in this encyclopedia teaches, arriving this time from the fangs: legitimacy and justice are not the same thing, respectability is no guarantee of fairness, and a court must be judged by what it does, not by the seal on its door or the blood on its floor. The vampires did one thing right. It does not make them good. It makes the Guild's pretensions a lie. Both of those things are true, and Waluigi will now go stand in some sunlight. WAH.

intelGains.reason: The tribunal reveals the Onyx Hand can be procedurally fair while remaining politically monstrous.
